question.text: Krishna Real Assets Fund (Cat II) is evaluating whether RTA appointment is mandatory. Which of the following is the CORRECT regulatory driver that has made RTA appointment compulsory for AIFs?

answer.text: SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996 applied mutatis mutandis to AIFs
SEBI Merchant Banker Regulations mandating RTA registration
Companies Act, 2013 Section 88 registering beneficial interest

Amendments to the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 via Finance Act, 2019 (effective 1-Jul-2020) notified RTAs as 'collecting agents' for stamp duty on issue, transfer and sale of AIF units, making RTA appointment compulsory to enable collection of applicable stamp duty

explanation.text: The Logic: The workbook explains that the Central Government, via amendments to the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 introduced by the Finance Act, 2019 effective 1 July 2020, notified RTAs to act as collecting agents. SEBI then stated that all registered RTAs shall act as collecting agents for stamp duty on the issue, transfer and sale of AIF units. Because this collection mechanism runs through the RTA, appointment of an RTA is compulsory for an AIF. The Trap: The Mutual Funds Regulations distractor wrongly imports the MF regime; nothing in the AIF Regulations is applied "mutatis mutandis" to mandate an RTA. The Merchant Banker distractor confuses RTA registration with merchant-banker registration. The Companies Act, Section 88 distractor cites a beneficial-interest register that is unrelated to the AIF RTA mandate. Note: The chain to remember is: Indian Stamp Act amendments (via Finance Act, 2019) -> RTAs notified as collecting agents -> SEBI circular confirming the same -> RTA appointment compulsory for AIFs to enable stamp-duty collection on units.
